Female Tasmanian devils attain an ultimate total length of 57 centimeters [Li = 57 centimeters], whereas males are notably larger, reaching an ultimate total length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size is among the most conspicuous traits of the species and has been well documented across multiple wild populations. The maximum recorded lifespan in captivity, measured under the stable thermal conditions of a controlled environment at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], reaches approximately 4745 days [am = approximately 4745 days], though individuals in the wild typically succumb much earlier due to disease, intraspecific aggression, and environmental pressures. Gestation is remarkably brief for a mammal of this size, with the interval between fertilisation and parturition lasting just 26 days [tg = 26 days] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].

At birth, the altricial neonate weighs a mere 0.0235 grams [Wwb = 0.0235 grams], a value that underscores the extreme altriciality typical of dasyurid marsupials. Following parturition, the newborn must crawl from the birth canal to the pouch, where it attaches to a teat for an extended period of lactation. The time since birth at weaning, marking the point of nutritional independence from the mother, occurs at 243 days [tx = 243 days] under captive conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that allows for substantial somatic growth within the pouch and during the early post-emergent juvenile phase. The wet weight at weaning for a successfully reared joey is approximately 200 grams [Wwx = approximately 200 grams], representing a considerable increase from the negligible birth mass but still far from the adult asymptotic mass. This protracted period of maternal investment is energetically costly for the female and is reflected in the species' relatively slow life-history pace compared to other mammals of comparable adult size.

Under the consistently warm thermal conditions of a controlled captive environment held at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], female devils typically produce a single litter of up to four young per birthing event [N_R_i = up to four young per birthing event], and they are capable of raising approximately 1.3 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.3 litters annually], reflecting the maximum observed reproductive output for the species. This breeding frequency is modest compared to many small-bodied dasyurids, which often exhibit semelparous or highly iteroparous strategies. The allocation of resources towards reproduction is constrained by the energy demands of lactation, as the growing pouch young require a rich milk supply for many months. Field records indicate that females in good body condition are more likely to successfully wean a full litter, whereas those facing nutritional stress may exhibit reduced litter sizes or complete reproductive failure.

The time since birth at puberty, representing the onset of sexual maturation, occurs at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth] under the standard thermal conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] in captivity. This relatively late attainment of reproductive maturity, equivalent to roughly two years of age, is a key feature of the species' life-history strategy. Once sexually mature, individuals typically breed annually. Reaching adulthood also coincides with the acquisition of a stable home range, which males defend aggressively during the breeding season.

The ultimate wet weight of an adult Tasmanian devil, measured as the asymptotic body mass attained by fully grown individuals, is approximately 6500 grams [Wwi = approximately 6500 grams]. This substantial body mass, combined with a powerful bite force, allows adult devils to consume nearly every part of a carcass, including bones, making them highly effective scavengers within their Tasmanian ecosystem. Disease outbreaks, particularly devil facial tumour disease, have caused severe population declines in recent decades, selectively impacting sexually mature adults and thereby altering the age structure of wild populations. Long-term monitoring studies continue to track changes in life-history parameters, such as survival rates and age at first reproduction, as the species adapts to this novel selective pressure. Conservation efforts rely on these demographic data to model population viability and guide management strategies for this iconic marsupial.
